sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot v, part 2 (printed pp. 182–192)
rows: [p. 182] Andab. Ingeniosam excogitasti fugam; sed quae ex alia parte in retia te reducat; facis enim motum telluris ab aqua esse, & tamen fortiorem esse motum terrae quam aquae, id est, plus in effectu quam in causa: nosti enim quod cursus diurnus praevenit cursum aestus, integra cottidie hora. [Margin: Motus terraene an maris sit velocior.]

[p. 182] Andab. A clever flight [fugam] you have devised; but one which from the other side would lead you back into the nets; for you make the motion of the earth [telluris] to be from the water, and yet the motion of the earth [terrae] to be stronger than [that] of the water, that is, more in the effect than in the cause: for you know that the diurnal course outruns [praevenit] the course of the tide [aestus] by a whole hour daily. [Margin: Whether the motion of the earth [terrae] or of the sea be the swifter.]

Ereu. Sed res ex opposito accidit: velocior enim longe est motio aestus (si hoc modo eam sumis) quod sic ostendo. Non vides aquam quam aestum dicimus gravitate sua versus medium globi tendere, non vides proinde eam [p. 183] in tellure sedere? non vides ergo tellure vehi, vel potius revehi? si igitur quantum tellus movetur, tantum ipsa retroagitur, & tamen contra telluris motum infra 25. horas totum ambitum perficit, 25. horis facit quod tellus 48. utrum iam credis velocius moveri.

Ereu. But the thing happens from the opposite: for far swifter is the motion [motio] of the tide (if you take it in this mode), which I show thus. Do you not see that the water which we call the tide [aestum] by its own heaviness [gravitate] tends toward the middle of the globe, do you not see accordingly that it [p. 183] sits on the earth [tellure]? do you not see therefore [that it is] carried [vehi] by the earth [tellure], or rather carried back [revehi]? if therefore as much as the earth [tellus] is moved, so much it itself is driven back [retroagitur], and yet against the motion of the earth [telluris] within 25 hours it completes the whole circuit [ambitum], in 25 hours it does what the earth [tellus] [does] in 48: which [of the two] do you now believe to be moved more swiftly?
Andab. Verum dicis.
Andab. You say true.

Ereu. Sed non vere, cum enim aquae cursus non ad mundum, sed ad ipsas dumtaxat terrae partes componatur, telluris autem partes ad mundum comparatae moventur, & non una respectu alterius; efficitur non propterea maiori motu seu velocitate opus esse aquae ut ad determinatam terrae partem perveniat, quia terra in oppositum fertur, quam si non omnino ferretur; sicut in musca rotam adversum ascendente, vel homine contra motum navis obambulante, notis exemplis perspectum est.

Ereu. But not truly; for since the course of the water is reckoned [componatur] not to the world, but only to the very parts of the earth [terrae], while the parts of the earth [telluris] are moved compared [comparatae] to the world, and not one in respect [respectu] of another; it is brought about [efficitur] that not on that account is there need to the water of a greater motion or speed [velocitate] in order that it may reach a determinate part of the earth [terrae] because the earth [terra] is carried [fertur] into the opposite [way], than if it were not carried at all; as, in a fly climbing a wheel the contrary way [adversum], or a man walking about [obambulante] against the motion of a ship, is seen through [perspectum est] by known examples.

Non tamen hoc sic affirmo ut telluris & maris oppositos conatus non sibi esse invicem impedimento velim; clarissimum enim est non posse aliter contingere: sed ut vectationem qua terra aquam vehit, nullum esse obicem tantummodo asseram.

Not however do I so affirm this, as that I would have [velim] the opposed endeavours [conatus] of the earth [telluris] and of the sea not be an impediment to each other in turn [invicem]; for it is most clear that it cannot happen otherwise: but [only] so that I may assert only [tantummodo] that the carriage [vectationem] by which the earth [terra] carries the water is no obstacle [obicem].

Ergo ut reipsa tuae difficultati satisfaciam, scito ex aestu argumentum desumi non posse velocitatis aquae. Cum (ut superius diximus eadem aqua non circumferatur toti terrae, vel si cir[p. 184]cumferatur, non sit in nostra potestate indagare quanto hoc tempore faciat: Sed neque vim aquae ex velocitate perpendi debere, cum aqua non motu recta progressivo feratur, sed sursum, deorsum & in latera; unde nihil certi statui potest. Tandem concesso tellurem velocius ferri quam mare, nihil incommodi esse admissum. Eadem enim virtus motrix corpus magis aptum motui plus pellit quam aliud minus aptum. Unde non est incommodum eandem vim, mediante aqua plus posse in terram non resistentem, quam in aquam resistentem. Et Galilaeus in dialogis de motu, docet tardissimam causam repetitione sui posse velocissimo motui originem dare; sicut & in mechanicis demonstrari solet quodlibet pondus qualibet vi moveri posse.

Therefore, that I may in the thing itself [reipsa] satisfy your difficulty, know [scito] that from the tide an argument of the speed of the water cannot be taken [desumi]. Since (as we said above the same water is not carried round [circumferatur] to the whole earth [terrae], or if it is [p. 184] carried round, it is not in our power to track down [indagare] in how much time it does this: But neither [know that] the force [vim] of the water ought to be weighed [perpendi] from the speed, since the water is carried not by a straight progressive [progressivo] motion, but upward, downward and to the sides; whence nothing certain can be established. Lastly, it being conceded that the earth [tellurem] is carried more swiftly than the sea, nothing inconvenient [incommodi] has been admitted. For the same motive virtue [virtus motrix] drives a body more apt for motion more than another less apt. Whence it is not inconvenient [incommodum] that the same force [vim], the water mediating [mediante aqua], can [do] more upon the earth [terram] not resisting than upon the water resisting. And Galileo in [his] dialogues on motion teaches that a most slow cause by repetition of itself can give origin to a most swift motion; as also in mechanics it is customarily demonstrated that any weight whatever can be moved by any force whatever.

Asphal. Est adhuc quod me sollicitum habet. Etsi enim quae hactenus dixisti, sic recte dicta existimem, ut posito mundi ordine vera sint, hoc tamen me retinet; haec principium habere non potuisse, & si non sit unde principium accipiant, neque continue durare posse. Forsitan obscurius locutus sum, rursus itaque me expono. Peto num si sol & tellus ponantur utraque quiescere, motus ex eorum situ incepturus sit, necne? Si enim dicas non secuturum, nescio quomodo mihi verisimile est motum quem posuisti, non habere radi[p. 185]cem
qua subsistat, & (quod sequitur) subito defecturum. Si autem secuturus sit, ex positione solis & terrae motus quem dixisti, hoc quomodo fiat aveo intelligere.

Asphal. There is still [something] which holds me anxious [sollicitum]. For although I reckon the things which you have said up to now so rightly said that, the order of the world being posited [posito mundi ordine], they are true, this nevertheless holds me back [retinet]: that these could not have had a beginning [principium], and, if there is not whence they may receive a beginning, [that they] cannot continually endure either. Perhaps I have spoken rather obscurely; so I set myself out [expono] again. I ask whether, if the sun and the earth [tellus] are posited both to be at rest [quiescere], motion is going to begin [incepturus sit] from their site [situ], or not? For if you say [it is] not going to follow, I know not how, [but] it is likely [verisimile] to me that the motion which you have posited does not have a root [p. 185] by which it may subsist, and (what follows) [that it is] going suddenly to fail. But if the motion which you have spoken of is going to follow from the position of the sun and the earth [terrae], how this may come about [fiat] I long [aveo] to understand.

Ereu. Quoniam de principio motus quaeris, necesse est principium fuisse concedas, & hoc quod inde constans est, solem & terram in determinato situ collocata esse: & quoniam hic situs ad libitum nobis est, esto sol in Aequatore fixus sic ut Insulam sancti Laurentis, vel aliam ex foelicibus illis terris quae post eam Insulam Lusitanis occurrunt perpendiculariter feriat, & quid ex his secuturum sit, pariter meditemur

Ereu. Since you ask about the beginning [principio] of motion, it is necessary that you concede there to have been a beginning, and this, which is consistent [constans] with that [inde]: that the sun and the earth [terram] were placed in a determinate site [situ]: and since this site is at our pleasure [ad libitum], let the sun be [esto] fixed in the Equator so that it strikes perpendicularly the Island of Saint Lawrence, or another of those happy lands which after that Island meet [occurrunt] the Portuguese [Lusitanis], and let us likewise consider [meditemur] what is going to follow from these [things]

Et ne te in devio sine duce videar derelinquere, Cum sol totum unum hemisphaerium illuminet, ex eodem vapores excitabit. Et quoniam eadem vis agens in passa diversae naturae, plus agit in illud quod ad actionem suscipiendam, magis est dispositum, Hemisphaerii in quod agit vultum intueamur. Et ecce imaginem. Non vides ex hac parte qua per Africam tenditur, in America longe plus terrae apparere, quam ex illa qua per mare Pacificum in eandem Americam pergitur? si itaque facilius vapores ex humido quam ex sicco resolvuntur, necesse est plures ex mari pacifico subire, & (quod ex hoc fit, motum vaporum, i. ventum suscitari: & mare venti talis motum sentire, & tellurem aquarum concussione in [p. 186] adversam partem pelli, Africamque ostendere soli. Et hoc toties futurum, quoties sol in has partes perpendiculariter inciderit. Unde vides ex ipsa dispositione telluris & solis fieri ut semper motus inexistat. [Margin: Quomodo incepit motus terrae?]

And lest I seem to abandon you in a pathless place [in devio] without a guide: Since the sun illuminates one whole hemisphere, from the same it will raise [excitabit] vapours. And since the same force [vis] acting upon patients [passa] of diverse nature acts more upon that which is more disposed to receiving the action, let us gaze upon the face [vultum] of the Hemisphere upon which it acts. And behold the image. Do you not see that on this side, by which [the way] stretches [tenditur] through Africa, in America far more land appears than on that by which one proceeds [pergitur] through the Pacific sea into the same America? if therefore vapours are resolved [resolvuntur] more easily from the moist [humido] than from the dry [sicco], it is necessary that more go up [subire] from the pacific sea, and (what comes about from this) that a motion of vapours, i.e. wind, is stirred up: and that the sea feels the motion of such a wind, and that the earth [tellurem] by the concussion [concussione] of the waters is [p. 186] driven into the adverse part, and shows Africa to the sun. And that this will be as often as the sun falls [inciderit] perpendicularly upon these parts. Whence you see that from the very disposition of the earth [telluris] and of the sun it comes about that motion is always in [it] [inexistat]. [Margin: How did the motion of the earth [terrae] begin?]
Andab. Recte si in ea parte collocatus sit sol: sed quid si in alia aliqua parte Aequatoris, vel extra Aequatorem?
Andab. Rightly, if the sun is placed in that part: but what if in some other part of the Equator, or outside the Equator?

Ereu. Siccine naturae & ipsius parenti hanc prudentiam negas ut solem telluremque collocent, ubi fini & operibus ipsorum maxime expedit? Sed si in alia parte collocata forent, motus semper ex inaequalitate partium aquosarum & terrestrium orietur, sed alia versum quem indagare non est hodierni otii sive negotii. Hoc proinde expedi mihi. Motum hunc telluris an praecise & Mathematice credas esse circularem?

Ereu. Is it thus [Siccine] you deny to nature and to its parent this prudence, that they should place the sun and the earth [tellurem] where it is most expedient for the end [fini] and the works of them? But if they were placed in another part, the motion would always arise [orietur] from the inequality of the watery and earthy parts, but toward another [direction] [alia versum], which to track down is not [a matter] of today's leisure or business [otii sive negotii]. This therefore disentangle [expedi] for me: this motion of the earth [telluris], do you believe [it] to be precisely and Mathematically circular?

Andab. Nihil minus. Cum enim Physice procreari hunc motum viderimus, Physicarum vero causarum quanta sit fragilitas & vicissitudo heri exposueris, satis mihi constat Mathematicum rigorem in hoc motu nullum esse posse, sed notabilem aliquem a circulo defectum cur ponam non video. [Margin: Motum terrae esse progressivum.]

Andab. Nothing less. For since we have seen this motion to be procreated Physically, and how great is the fragility and vicissitude of Physical causes you expounded yesterday, it is sufficiently established [constat] to me that there can be no Mathematical rigour in this motion; but why I should posit any notable deficiency [defectum] from the circle I do not see. [Margin: That the motion of the earth [terrae] is progressive [progressivum].]

Ereu. Penitus inspicito causas motus, & vide qua motionem agant & vim suam exprimant. Aquam quae ex pacifico eiicitur non vides turgere supra aliam, ut possit eam [p. 187] movere? qualis est hic motus, circularis, an rectus?

Ereu. Look thoroughly into [Penitus inspicito] the causes of the motion, and see by what [way] [qua] they perform [agant] the motion [motionem] and express their force. The water which is cast out [eiicitur] from the pacific, do you not see it swell [turgere] above the other, so that it may be able to [p. 187] move it? of what kind is this motion, circular, or straight?
Andab. Vel rectus, vel certe versus rectum: recedit enim a circulo quantum super aliam elevatur: sed respectu circuli non est notabilis tam exilis elevatio.
Andab. Either straight, or certainly toward straight: for it recedes from the circle as much as it is raised above the other: but in respect of the circle so slender an elevation is not notable.
Ereu. Bene est; sed singuli fluctus subiectam sibi aquam quomodo feriunt?
Ereu. It is well; but the single waves [fluctus], how do they strike the water placed under them?
Andab. Videntur sic se percutere, sicut planum sphaeram, vel tangens linea circulum (si moveretur) feriret.
Andab. They seem to strike [se percutere] thus, as a plane would strike a sphere, or a tangent line a circle (if it were moved).
Ereu. Pone rotam in plano, & supra aliud planum per modum tangentis ei cum impetu applicato, quorsum versus movebitur rota?
Ereu. Place a wheel on a plane, and above [it] another plane applied to it in the manner of a tangent with impetus: toward where [quorsum versus] will the wheel be moved?

Andab. Recta quidem procedet, sed sic ut circa suum centrum semper moveatur, sed hoc inde accidere crediderim quod gravitas eam sua tellure figat. Unde cum motus ex una tantum parte incumbat, praecipitat quasi partes tactas; si autem in rota esset aliud agens subtus rota, motu adverso quasi subtrahens inferiores partes quantum causa superior eas partes porro agit, crederem perfecto circulo latum iri rotam. Et hoc ipsum ad amussim in terra contingere iam declaratum est. Undique enim eam flagellant aquae, & quantum unae in Orientem, tantum alterae in Occidentem propellunt.

Andab. It will proceed straight [Recta] indeed, but so that it is always moved about its own centre; but this I would believe to happen from this, that heaviness [gravitas] fixes it to its own earth [tellure]. Whence, since the motion bears [incumbat] from one part only, it hurls forward [praecipitat] as it were the parts touched; but if there were in the wheel another agent beneath the wheel, by a contrary motion as it were drawing away [subtrahens] the lower parts as much as the superior cause drives [agit] those parts forward [porro], I would believe that the wheel would be carried [latum iri] in a perfect circle. And that this very thing happens exactly [ad amussim] in the earth [terra] has already been declared. For on all sides the waters lash it, and as much as the ones drive [it] forward into the East, so much the others into the West.
[p. 188] Ereu. Si itaque tellus ex una parte fixa poneretur, dum ex alia protruditur, rem factam haberemus.
[p. 188] Ereu. If therefore the earth [tellus] were posited fixed from one part, while from the other it is thrust forward [protruditur], we would have the thing done [rem factam].
Andab. Plane haberes.
Andab. Plainly you would have [it].
Ereu. At motum ipsum circularem (vel impetum potius) successive inceptum fuisse etiam te credere existimo.
Ereu. But that the circular motion itself (or rather the impetus) was begun successively [successive], I reckon that you too believe.
Andab. Nequaquam, Deus enim causis omnibus paratis indidit motum perfectum primo instanti.
Andab. By no means; for God, all the causes having been prepared, put into [them] [indidit] a perfect motion in the first instant.

Ereu. Si modo possibile sit, non desunt enim qui motum non per infinitos tarditatis gradus ex quietis abysso ascendere impossibile prorsus reputant. Sed hoc non tangit nos. Si enim Deus immediate motum indidit, nihil dubium quin eum indiderit, qui suae intentioni maxime consentaneus erat, & qui ex causis ad hoc natis perpetuitatem sortiretur: quare ex ea parte rem factam etiam sic haberemus: sed fac eam ex causis naturalibus explicatis ortum habuisse. Tunc necesse erit motum maris in una parte telluris exordio capto, ad caeteras sensim pervenisse.

Ereu. If only it be possible; for there are not lacking those who reckon it altogether impossible for motion to ascend from the abyss of rest not through infinite degrees of slowness [tarditatis]. But this does not touch us. For if God put in motion immediately, [there is] nothing doubtful but that he put in that which was most consonant [consentaneus] to his intention, and which from causes born for this would obtain [sortiretur] perpetuity: wherefore from that side also we would thus have the thing done: but suppose [fac] it to have had [its] origin from the natural causes [already] explicated. Then it will be necessary that the motion of the sea, a beginning having been taken in one part of the earth [telluris], reached the others little by little [sensim].
Andab. Si de motu maris loqueris nihil dubium.
Andab. If you speak of the motion of the sea, nothing doubtful.
Ereu. Neque hoc igitur dubium alias maris partes interea (seu cum primo impetus ad eas deferretur) restitisse motui.
Ereu. Nor therefore [is] this doubtful, that other parts of the sea meanwhile (or when the impetus was first carried down [deferretur] to them) resisted the motion.
Andab. Certum est.
Andab. It is certain.

[p. 189] Ereu. Quid ergo obstat quin dum crearetur, in una parte telluris ab aquis impetus, aliam resistentem ponamus, donec integre superata est: Et quod connexum esse fassus es, protrudi tellurem prorsum.

[p. 189] Ereu. What then stands in the way [obstat] that, while the impetus was being created by the waters in one part of the earth [telluris], we should posit another [part] resisting, until it was [est] entirely overcome: And, which you have confessed to be connected [with it], that the earth [tellurem] is thrust forward [protrudi] straight on [prorsum].
Andab. Hoc, quod una pars terrae sine alia moveri non possit, neque impetum suscipere.
Andab. This: that one part of the earth [terrae] cannot be moved without another, nor receive impetus.
Ereu. Neque tremere credis unam telluris partem sine alia?
Ereu. Do you not believe either that one part of the earth [telluris] trembles without another?
Andab. Immo vero: nimiis hoc experimentis constat.
Andab. Nay indeed [Immo vero]: this is established by too many [nimiis] experiments.

Ereu. Cur non itaque versus aliquam partem concuti? quod est impetum concipere, & est motus quaedam species vel inceptio. Nunc itaque si quid obstat, dicito; alioquin habes quod petiisti; tellurem ex una parte fixam, & per consequens ex ea parte qua movetur quasi in rectum porrici.

Ereu. Why not therefore [that it is] shaken toward some part? which is to conceive impetus, and is a certain species or beginning [inceptio] of motion. Now therefore, if anything stands in the way, say [it] [dicito]; otherwise you have what you sought [petiisti]: that the earth [tellurem] [is] fixed from one part, and consequently [per consequens] from that part by which it is moved is stretched forth [porrici] as it were into a straight [line].
Andab. Saltem postquam tota impetum concepit, evanescat haec ratio, & subtrahetur inferius quod superne adiicitur.
Andab. At least after the whole has conceived impetus, let this reason [ratio] vanish, and that which is added [adiicitur] above will be drawn away [subtrahetur] below.

Ereu. Aliquid dandum est modo quo inceptus est motus, in cuius naturam facile concedit causa non opposita. Sed aliud considera, nempe quod quies ad motum, hoc etiam, dempta proportione, esse debiliorem motum ad potentiorem: habet itaque etiam pars debilius mota naturam resistentis, & parti[p. 190]bus ubi dominatur Ventus antipus obsistet plaga. Semper itaque causa eadem constat, & effectus proinde similis expectandus est.

Ereu. Something must be granted to the mode in which the motion was begun, into whose nature a cause not opposed easily yields [concedit]. But consider another [thing], namely that what rest [is] to motion, this also, proportion being taken away [dempta proportione], a weaker motion is to a more powerful [one]: therefore the part moved more weakly also has the nature of a resisting [thing], and to the parts [p. 190] where the Wind dominates the antipodal [antipus] region [plaga] will stand opposed [obsistet]. Always therefore the same cause stands [constat], and accordingly a similar effect is to be expected.
Andab. Tu vero, Asphali, credo interea dormis, neque quicquam tibi metuis ab hoc sole qui nos saltabundos dicam, an volantes toto caelo agit.
Andab. But you, Asphalius, I believe, are sleeping meanwhile, and fear nothing for yourself from this sun which drives us, dancing [saltabundos] shall I say, or flying, through the whole heaven.

Asphal. Non dormio, Andabata, sed nimium quam delector Astrorum socius & iam caeligena, & gratiam non mediocrem habeo Copernico qui nos fecit omnes Caelicolas, omnes supera astra tenentes. Unum est quod me male habet, quod si haec, quae inter vos pacti estis, constent, frigore perituri simus. Nescio enim quomodo terra sese unquam poterit ab Aequatoris extricare semita: Aquam enim sub Aequinoctiali maximam & potentissimam cernimus, per eam itaque totum orbem nostrum diriget.

Asphal. I am not sleeping, Andabata, but I am delighted beyond measure [nimium quam], a companion of the Stars and now heaven-born [caeligena], and I have no middling thanks [gratiam] to Copernicus, who has made us all Heaven-dwellers [Caelicolas], all holding the stars above [supera astra tenentes]. One thing there is which troubles me [me male habet]: that, if these [things] which you have agreed [pacti estis] between you hold good [constent], we are going to perish of cold. For I do not know how the earth [terra] will ever be able to extricate itself from the path [semita] of the Equator: for the water under the Equinoctial we perceive [to be] greatest and most powerful; through it [per eam] therefore it will direct our whole globe [orbem].
Ereu. Quid futurum foret si Aequinoctiali tramite sol nusquam aberraret, non ausim promittere, cum uterque Polus constanti, nos, caeso per aequales tenebras lumine uteremur.

Ereu. What would be going to happen if the sun nowhere strayed from the Equinoctial track [tramite], I would not dare to promise, since each Pole would use a constant [light], we a light cut [caeso] by equal darknesses.

Hoc scio vel foeliciorem esse hodiernam mundi posituram, vel certe magis nobis proficuam, eo quod animos ab aviditate terrestrium plus absterreat, vel certe absterrere nata sit. Tu modo ne solis ea lege decursus [p. 191] fiat, ne verere. Ad terrarum dumtaxat quam prae manibus habes tabulam conversus, Maiorianas fauces consule, vel Drakianas potius. Hunc enim freti Transmagellanici authorem & nostras fama, & antiqua quam vidi navigationis ipsius delineatio, & Hispani dum adhuc illud esse pernegarent, testati sunt. [Margin: Motum telluris sub Zodiaco esse.]

This I know: either that the present [hodiernam] placing [posituram] of the world is happier, or certainly more profitable to us, in that it frightens [absterreat] minds away more from greed for earthly things, or certainly is apt by nature [nata sit] to frighten [them] away. Only do not you fear lest the running-down [decursus] of the sun [p. 191] should come about by that law. Only turning to the map [tabulam] of the lands which you have at hand, consult the Mairean straits [Maiorianas fauces], or rather the Drakean. For of this [man as] author of the Transmagellanic strait, both the report [fama] of our country [nostras], and an old delineation of his navigation which I have seen, and the Spaniards, while they still utterly denied that it existed, have testified. [Margin: That the motion of the earth [telluris] is under the Zodiac.]
Asphal. Abunde respondisti.
Asphal. You have answered abundantly.
Andab. Esto, sed hae fauces mihi nihil fabulantur non plusquam Indis Hispanorum in primo adventu characteres.
Andab. Be it so; but these straits [fauces] tell [fabulantur] me nothing, no more than the characters [characteres] of the Spaniards [told] the Indians at [their] first arrival.

Asphal. Non vides aquas telluris impultrices, per has angustias quae ad Austrum inclinatae sunt, ad Orientem & Aequatorem, unde refluant, oblique proficisci? quare & impulsam tellurem non recta sed declinato versari necesse est. Finge modo tellurem in coniunctione Zodiaci cum Aequatore positam & aestima quanam vergat recta illa tangens secundum quam promoturas tellurem aquas praedixisti.

Asphal. Do you not see that the waters, impellers [impultrices] of the earth [telluris], through these narrows [angustias] which are inclined toward the South, set out obliquely toward the East and the Equator, whence they may flow back? wherefore it is necessary that the earth [tellurem] too, impelled, turns [versari] not straight but in a declined [direction] [declinato]. Now imagine [Finge] the earth [tellurem] placed at the conjunction of the Zodiac with the Equator, and estimate where [quanam] that straight tangent line inclines [vergat], according to which you foretold the waters were going to move forward [promoturas] the earth [tellurem].
Andab. Video, sed idem video hunc circulum a Zodiaco satis dissidere, per quem tamen ferri progressivo incessu terram uterque profitemini.

Andab. I see; but likewise I see this circle to differ [dissidere] sufficiently from the Zodiac, through which nevertheless you both profess the earth [terram] to be carried with a progressive gait [progressivo incessu].
Ereu. Sed vide ne non parallelus vel instar paralleli sit.
Ereu. But see whether it be not [ne non] parallel, or like a parallel.
Andab. Video posse esse: sed sit necne, [p. 192] non satis dispicio.
Andab. I see it can be: but whether it is or not, [p. 192] I do not sufficiently discern.
Asphal. Attende haec littora Austrina Beachi & Maleturi nominibus signata, quibus obsessum mare in Aequatorem vel certe in pacificum agitur.
Asphal. Attend to these Southern [Austrina] shores marked with the names of Beach and Maletur, by which the sea, hemmed in [obsessum], is driven into the Equator, or certainly into the pacific.
Andab. Video sed tune fidem facis, Asphali, Ereunium hunc non pictorem corrupisse, ut commentis suis gloriam circumdaret? Adeo conspirare videntur.

Andab. I see; but do you give assurance [fidem facis], Asphalius, that this Ereunius has not corrupted the painter [pictorem], so that he might surround his fictions [commentis] with glory? So much do they seem to conspire.

Ereu. Ego fidem facio me commenta, ut vocas, mea fidei tabularum adaptavisse, quod tantumdem est. Tellus itaque, quibus profatus sum lenociniis prolecta solem in sua distantia sub eo quem Zodiacum appellamus, stellarum circulo, quotannis succingit.

Ereu. I give assurance [fidem facio] that I have adapted my fictions [commenta], as you call [them], to the credit [fidei] of the maps [tabularum], which is just as much [tantumdem]. The earth [tellus] therefore, enticed [prolecta] by the allurements [lenociniis] which I have uttered [profatus sum], girds [succingit] the sun yearly, at its own distance, under that circle of stars which we call the Zodiac.

terms: motio = the act of moving; motus = the motion
White uses both of the tide; motio bracketed to keep them apart.
Relative motion: the water's course is measured against the earth's parts, the earth's against the world (cf. Galileo's fly/ship examples).
The earth's carrying of the water, the core of White's tidal–rotational mechanism.
Scholastic term for the power of a mover; cf. glossary 'virtue'.
Scholastic 'medium' of causal action: the water transmits the force to the earth.
Probably the Discorsi, Day 3, on acceleration from rest through infinite degrees of slowness; also Galileo's mechanics, where any weight can be moved by any force.
Asphalius' objection concerns a temporal beginning of the motion, not a logical principle.
The 'root' by which the motion subsists = its sustaining cause.
The Portuguese name (São Lourenço). Madagascar is not in fact on the equator; White's hypothetical sun is fixed 'so that' it strikes those lands perpendicularly.
Here: motion always inheres in the earth–sun system. See glossary.
in mathematical exactness / according to natural causes
The scholastic contrast between mathematical idealization and the imprecision of physical causes.
Deviation of the earth's path from a true circle; not an eclipse.
Aristotelian 'progressive motion' (De incessu animalium); White applies it to the earth's annual motion, which moves forward rather than returning on itself.
Impetus theory; Ereunius equates conceiving impetus with a beginning of motion.
quies ad motum … debilior motus ad potentiorem
what rest is to motion … a weaker motion is to a more powerful
rest resists motion; analogously, slower motion resists faster
Dempta proportione = 'allowing for the difference of degree'.
antipus may qualify Ventus ('counter-wind') or plaga; plaga = region or blow
Greek ἀντίπους, 'with feet opposite'; see notes.
heaven-born / Heaven-dwellers / holding the stars above
Mock-epic praise of Copernicus: the earth, now a planet, makes its inhabitants dwellers in the heavens.
the celestial equator; the terrestrial equator
Strait of Le Maire (1616) / Drake Passage
Le Maire's and Drake's southern passages beyond the Strait of Magellan.
the passage south of Tierra del Fuego
Drake (1578) was credited by English report with finding open sea south of Magellan's strait; White cites English report, an old chart of Drake's voyage, and Spanish denial.
Allusion to Amerindians' first encounter with European writing.
Rare feminine agent noun (impultrix) agreeing with aquae.
From Marco Polo's Locach/Maletur, shown on Mercator and Ortelius maps on the coast of Terra Australis.
Ironic erotic metaphor: the earth lured to 'gird' the sun.
Punning with fidei tabularum, 'the credit of the maps'.

Ingeniosam excogitasti fugam’ (p. 182, margin ‘Motus terraene an maris sit velocior’) to Ereunius' ‘…stellarum circulo, quotannis succingit.’ (p. 192). Knot vi (‘Cur tellus axem parallelum axi aequatoris teneat’) begins on p. 192 with ‘Asphal. Sic me uno absolvis dubio’, beside its marginal title.
Offset +11 holds (signatures Aa p. 185, Aa ij p. 187, Aa iij p. 189). Pages 188 and 189 are short (lower part blank in the scan) but the text runs on without a gap.

Marginal notes: p. 182 ‘Motus terraene an maris sit velocior’; p. 185 ‘Quomodo incepit motus terrae?’; p. 186 ‘Motum terrae esse progressivum’; p. 190 ‘Motum telluris sub Zodiaco esse’ (printed ‘Motū’). Each placed at the end of the speech it stands beside.

Uncertain readings / interpretations: (a) p. 183 ‘25.’ (twice) — the italic 5 resembles a long s; read as 25 (a lunar tidal day of c. 24h50m). (b) p. 184 the parenthesis opened at ‘(ut superius diximus’ is never closed in the print; kept. (c) p. 185 ‘meditemur Et ne te’ — no stop printed; kept. (d) p. 185 ‘ex hac parte qua per Africam tenditur, in America …’ — construed as the hemisphere seen from the African side; ‘in America’ may instead go with ‘tenditur’ (‘stretches through Africa into America’). (e) p. 190 ‘Ventus antipus obsistet plaga’ — ‘antipus’ (ἀντίπους, antipodal) is construed with plaga (‘the antipodal region will stand opposed’); alternatively ‘the counter-wind [Ventus antipus]’ with plaga = ‘blow’: ‘to the parts where the counter-wind dominates the blow will meet opposition’. {?antipus} not found elsewhere. (f) p. 190 ‘per eam … diriget’ — eam may be the water or the semita of the Equator; subject of diriget taken as the water. (g) p. 187 the speech ‘Recta quidem procedet … propellunt’ is printed under Andabata although its last two sentences sound like Ereunius; kept as printed. (h) p. 191 the speech ‘Non vides aquas telluris impultrices …’ is printed under Asphalius though it ends ‘praedixisti’; kept. (i) p. 191 a wide space after ‘fama’ — no letter missing on the image; read ‘nostras fama’ (‘the report of our country’).

Verification pass (sentence by sentence against the Latin and page images): no omissions or additions remaining; 5 corrections — (1) p. 186 ‘sed notabilem aliquem a circulo defectum cur ponam non video’ first drafted as if Andabata posited a notable deviation; corrected to ‘why I should posit any notable deficiency … I do not see’; (2) p. 183 ‘sed ut vectationem … nullum esse obicem tantummodo asseram’ restructured so that the carriage itself is the subject of ‘is no obstacle’; (3) p. 184 ‘nescio quomodo mihi verisimile est’ first drafted as ‘I do not know how it is likely’, corrected to the idiomatic ‘I know not how, [but] it is likely’; (4) transcription: a corrupted character in ‘telluremque’ (p. 186) corrected against the image; (5) p. 190 ‘Tu modo ne … fiat, ne verere’ corrected from an imperative ‘do not let…’ to ‘do not fear lest…’.

Conventions: as in glossary.md — long s → s, ligatures expanded, accents dropped, consonantal u → v; spellings kept (foelicibus, cottidie, authorem, littora, caeteras); supplied English words in [square brackets]; Latin of technical or ambiguous words in [brackets]; printed page changes marked [p. n]; tellus/terra distinguished by bracketing.
